enrichment.short_title: Non-party costs order against patent litigation funder Princo under section 51
key_facts: Philips sued Aventi for patent infringement over unlicensed CD-R discs; Princo GmbH funded Aventi's defence and gave a royalty indemnity but withdrew funding about six weeks before Aventi entered insolvent liquidation.
Jacob J permitted joinder of Princo and Mr Kuo so Philips could seek a non-party costs order under section 51 Supreme Court Act 1981.
Princo had a direct commercial interest in the English proceedings and causally funded Aventi's defence; Mr Kuo did not personally fund Aventi.
Philips sought costs of both the Aventi action and the section 51 application, including against Mr Kuo personally.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application at the conclusion of patent infringement proceedings for a non-party costs order against the funder and its managing director, with leave to appeal granted on the Princo order.
enrichment.outcome: Princo ordered to pay Philips' costs of the Aventi action save insofar as increased by claims relating to Fornet/Fornex and other non-Princo discs; Mr Kuo's personal section 51 application failed and he was awarded his costs of that application; no interim costs order; permission to appeal granted on compelling grounds.
enrichment.ratio: A commercially interested funder who causally enables an impecunious defendant to defend litigation for its own benefit may be ordered to pay the successful party's costs under section 51, distinguishing pure/disinterested funders immune after Hamilton v Al Fayed; funding must be causative and the order remains exceptional and discretionary.
legal_issues: Whether Princo was a pure or commercially interested funder
Whether Princo's funding was causative of Aventi's defence
Scope of a non-party costs order where only part of the claim related to third-party manufacturers' products
Personal liability of Mr Kuo where he did not provide funds
Costs of the section 51 application where joint representation was used

enrichment.short_title: Section 73(8) certificate quashed but Article 8 removal claim refused
key_facts: Indian asylum seeker married a British citizen and had a British child; his asylum appeal was treated as abandoned after non-attendance in August 2001.

In June 2002 he applied again on Article 8 grounds; the Secretary of State refused removal reconsideration and certified under section 73(8) that the application was made to delay removal with no other legitimate purpose.
His wife had learning disabilities and asthma; the Secretary of State considered she could accompany him to India or remain while he applied for entry clearance from abroad.
Judicial review challenged both the Article 8 refusal and the section 73(8) certificate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Secretary of State decisions following refusal on the papers and renewed permission before Maurice Kay J; permission to appeal granted to the Secretary of State.
enrichment.outcome: Challenge to the Article 8 removal decision dismissed; section 73(8) certificate quashed; no order as to costs; permission to appeal granted.
enrichment.ratio: Section 73(8) requires the decision-maker to ask whether the application was in reality a delaying tactic, not merely whether the claim could have been raised earlier or is hopeless; on the facts the certificate was flawed because the Secretary of State applied the wrong legal test.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'no other legitimate purpose' in section 73(8)(b)
Whether Article 8 was engaged by removal of a recently formed family
Whether temporary family separation for entry clearance was a proportionate Article 8(2) interference
Interaction between one-stop appeal procedure and post-determination applications
Correct approach following conflicting first-instance authorities (Vemenac, Balamurali, Ngamguem, Alia)

enrichment.short_title: Lloyd's underwriters' negligent misstatement claim against Coutts over HMU client account letter dismissed
key_facts: Lloyd's syndicates gave binding authorities to Hilton Malcolm Underwriting Ltd (HMU), expecting a separate client account at Coutts for underwriting monies.

Underwriters subscribed to a second binding authority in January 1996 and later suffered losses when HMU failed.

enrichment.short_title: Recoverability of marine recovery agent fees after Eurasian Dream fire judgment
key_facts: After a fire on Eurasian Dream, Cresswell J held the vessel owners liable and ordered assessment of WK Webster & Co fees as recoverable costs.

enrichment.short_title: Portsmouth FC option price reduced by full Milton Lane Allowance where Council consent price was nil
key_facts: Developer Sellar granted Portsmouth City Football Club an option to buy stadium expansion land for £2m less a Milton Lane Allowance of £1.1m minus X, where X was Council-identified consideration for consent to cross Milton Lane with the Spine Road.
The Council ultimately sold Barwood Land and Milton Lane freehold to the Developer for £4,255,000 in one conveyance without apportionment.
Both parties understood crossing Milton Lane required highway authority consent; counsel advised the Council could not demand a ransom for that consent.
The Club exercised the option and sought a declaration that the purchase price was £900,000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited Part 8 claim for declaratory relief on contractual purchase price before contractual completion date.
enrichment.ratio: On the natural meaning of the amended option clause, X related to the Council's consent as highway authority to cross Milton Lane; where the Council effectively identified nil consideration for that consent, the full £1.1m Milton Lane Allowance applies, and the Developer cannot rely on its own breach of the joint negotiation obligation to defeat the deduction.
legal_issues: Construction of 'consent for the Spine Road to cross Milton Lane'
Whether X could be nil or required apportionment of the £4.255m global price
Developer breach of clause 13 negotiation obligation
Whether the contract was frustrated or required Sudbrook-style gap-filling valuation
Apportionment methodology if consent had wider meaning

key_facts: Affluent ancillary relief proceedings in the Principal Registry; the husband appeared in person and the wife was legally represented.

enrichment.short_title: Limitation amendment allowed for solicitors' duty to advise on commercial wisdom of business purchase
key_facts: Claimants bought a business in March 1995 with solicitors Roddam acting; the business failed and they consulted Brysons from 1997 but did not issue until January 2001.

Original particulars alleged failure to advise against purchase and conveyancing-related negligence; proposed amendments pleaded a broader duty to advise on commercial wisdom, client vulnerability and specific warnings by Miss Smith.
The defence denied any duty to advise on wisdom of the transaction but pleaded warnings given in October 1994 and February 1995.
Judge Behrens allowed some amendments but refused others as raising new causes of action after limitation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of late amendments under CPR 17.4(2) after expiry of limitation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; specified amendments permitted; claimants 60% of costs below; appeal costs in the case.
enrichment.ratio: Amendments raising a duty to advise on commercial wisdom arose out of substantially the same facts already in issue on the original pleadings and defence (including pleaded warnings and denial of advisory duty), so CPR 17.4(2)/section 35 jurisdiction existed and discretion should be exercised to permit trial of the real issues despite delay.

Whether new claims arose from the same or substantially the same facts already in issue
Goode v Martin Human Rights Act-compliant reading of CPR 17.4(2)
Exercise of discretion where claim was already stale

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Amec carried out Tudor Street works under a letter of intent pending an amended JCT Design and Build 1998 contract.
The letter said terms including the arbitration agreement would be as in the proposed JCT form with the employer's tender schedule amendments.
The schedule named George Ashworth as adjudicator; Amec obtained a decision from adjudicator Mr Biscoe and brought Part 8 enforcement proceedings.

Whether amended JCT terms including adjudicator nomination were incorporated
Scope of Article 6A exception for adjudication enforcement disputes

enrichment.short_title: GP's strike-out application refused in parents' libel claim over surgery notice
key_facts: Parents of Robert Powell, who died aged 10 from undiagnosed Addison's disease in 1990, sued GPs over a 6 November 1992 surgery notice calling their HTV allegations lies and fantasy.
The claim was issued in 1995-1996; only Dr Williams remained as defendant after others were discontinued.
Dr Williams applied to strike out for delay, abuse of process and Article 6 unreasonable time, conceding a triable issue on malice but not on qualified privilege alone.
Proceedings were repeatedly stayed pending police/CPS investigations; claimants acted in person with a non-compliant Reply raising serious dishonesty allegations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to strike out or stay long-running Queen's Bench libel action.
enrichment.outcome: Strike-out application refused; parties invited to address further directions.
enrichment.ratio: Although delay was inordinate and a trial would not be within a reasonable time under Article 6, the delay was largely excusable because claimants reasonably awaited public investigations; a fair trial remained possible on documents and striking out would disproportionately interfere with the claimants' access to justice.
